chunks: BJT vs MOSFET comparison. The question: What is the difference between a BJT and MOSFET?
A BJT and a MOSFET both let a small control signal switch or shape a larger current. The key difference is the control. A BJT is controlled by a current into its base.
A MOSFET is controlled by a voltage on its gate, which draws almost no steady current.
That leads to different strengths: BJTs for precision analog, and MOSFETs for switching and digital logic.
Picture two ways of steering a boat. With a BJT, a person must keep pushing on the tiller the whole time to hold the course. That takes steady effort.
With a MOSFET, you set the rudder with a quick nudge and it stays there, with almost no ongoing effort.
The analogy breaks down since a MOSFET gate does need a brief pulse of charge each time you switch it.
At every current the BJT has more transconductance.

The BJT line is a straight line of slope 1 ( g m proportional to I C ); the MOSFET follows the same slope at very low current (weak inversion, with a ratio 1 over n lower) then bends over to a square-root law ( g m proportional to square root of I D ) in strong inversion.
At 1 milliamps the BJT has 38. 7 mS versus 6. 3 mS for this MOSFET (overdrive square root of 2I D over k equals 0. 32 volts).

A bigger device (higher W over L ) raises the square-root branch and keeps the MOSFET in weak inversion up to higher currents, so its g m gets closer to the BJT's (but never above I D over (nV T) ), which is why analogue MOS designers use large, low-current devices when they need gain per milliamp.
Current-controlled: the output is set by a steady input current. Voltage-controlled: the output is set by an input voltage with almost no current.
Gate: the MOSFET's control terminal, insulated from the channel. R DS(on) : the resistance of an on MOSFET, which can be a few milliohms.
Saturation voltage ( V CE(sat) ): the small voltage left across a fully on BJT, about 0. 1 to 0. 3 volts.
Take the example used further down this page: switching 5 amps. A fully on BJT keeps about 0. 3 volts across it, so it wastes 0. 3 times 5 equals 1. 5 watts.
It also needs about 0. 5 amps of steady base current (a gain of 10), which wastes roughly another 0. 35 watts. A MOSFET with an R DS(on) of 10 milliohms wastes 5 squared times 0.
01 equals 0. 25 watts, and it needs no steady gate current. That is the whole idea.
"A BJT is current-controlled: base current into a forward-biased junction controls collector current, with a gain around 100.
A MOSFET is voltage-controlled, with an insulated gate that draws essentially no DC current.
The BJT has higher transconductance per milliamp, better matching and lower noise, so it suits precision analogue.
The MOSFET has very low on-resistance, no base drive, positive temperature coefficient for current sharing, and scales to VLSI, so it dominates switching and digital."
